name: Mapia
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Arnold, Laura. 2025. Language as a lens into the prehistory of West New Guinea. Ch. 3 in [West New Guinea volume], ANU Press, p. 69.
sources.note: Nothing; status note only: Mapia belongs to the Micronesian branch of Oceanic (Jackson 1983; Marck 1994), is now extinct (last speaker died in the 1990s), and the atoll is now Biak-speaking.

sources.citation: Bender, Byron W., Ward H. Goodenough, Frederick H. Jackson, Jeffrey C. Marck, Kenneth L. Rehg, Ho-min Sohn, Stephen Trussel & Judith W. Wang. 2003. Proto-Micronesian reconstructions 1 and 2. Oceanic Linguistics 42(1): 1-110; 42(2): 271-358.
sources.note: Nothing on Mapian stress; 'Map, Old Mapian (Kubary 1889)' is a source language (p. 3) and about a dozen Map forms are cited in the cognate sets (yarmat 'person', maa 'die', naha 'child', ma-ram 'moon', yya 'rainbow', jerual 'month name', etc.), without accents.

sources.citation: Huizinga, F. 1996. De Mapia-kwestie. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 152(3): 429-460.
sources.note: Historical account of Mapia's 19th-century population and sources; may cite further early wordlists (e.g. from Dutch/German visitors) of the Micronesian language.
sources.venue: Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde

sources.citation: Stokhof, W. A. L. & Alma E. Almanar (eds). 1987. Holle lists: vocabularies in languages of Indonesia, Vol. 11: Celebes, Alor, Ambon, Irian Jaya, Madura and Lombok. Pacific Linguistics D-81. Mapia list (KITLV Or. 421/2(2), 1911 printing), pp. 253-261.
sources.note: Nothing; a bare numbered wordlist (Dutch orthography) with no stress marks and no notes on the collector, date or transcription.

sources.citation: Jackson, Frederick H. 1986. On determining the external relationships of the Micronesian languages. In P. Geraghty, L. Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), FOCAL II: Papers from the Fourth International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, 201-238. Pacific Linguistics C-94.
sources.note: Nothing; Mapia appears only in the list of Trukic languages on p. 201 ('the former language of the island of Mapia, about 100 miles north of Irian Jaya') and in the abbreviation list (MAP Old Mapian).

sources.citation: Jackson, Frederick H. 1984. Reflexes of Proto-Oceanic in the Trukic languages of Micronesia. In B. W. Bender (ed.), Studies in Micronesian Linguistics, 259-280. Pacific Linguistics C-80.
sources.note: Nothing; endnote 3 (end of article) only says Goodenough & Sugita 1980 identified the earlier language of Mapia as Trukic without evidence and that 'Old Mapian does appear Micronesian' (see also Bender 1975).

sources.citation: Jackson, Frederick Henry. 1983. The internal and external relationships of the Trukic languages of Micronesia. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (UMI 8408964), xix+460 pp. §4.5 'The position of Old Mapian', pp. 404-412, Table 28 'Old Mapian forms (after Kubary 1889)'; also p. 63 n. 11, p. 337 n. 43.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: No statement about Mapian stress. §4.5 re-analyses Kubary's data for consonant reflexes of PMc phonemes, the subject/possessive pronoun paradigms and the numerals, and concludes Old Mapian was probably a Nuclear Trukic language that separated about the same time as Woleaian. The dissertation's only stress remarks (pp. ~150, ~300) concern Proto-Trukic vowel developments, not Mapian. Reproduces Kubary's accent marks in Table 28 without comment.

sources.citation: Kubary, J. S. 1889 [in the volume Ethnographische Beiträge zur Kenntnis des Karolinen Archipels, Leiden: P. W. M. Trap, issued in 3 parts 1889-1895]. 'Notizen über einen Ausflug nach den westlichen Karolinen', pp. 79-114; Bunäj/Mapia section pp. 101-114, vocabulary, verb paradigms and numerals pp. 112-113.
sources.note: Nothing explicit. The ~130-item Bunäj vocabulary (pp. 112-113) prints acute accents on many forms (Jáñol 'chief', Yármat 'person', Féfin 'woman', Náha 'child', Kóčou 'rain', Méher 'sleep', hólu 'three', Ébugi '100' vs Fekáf 'evening', Ligín 'bark', Gagén 'trunk', Limék '50', Onék '60', Fihík '70', Tiék '90', Kanáñ 'there'), but nowhere in the volume are the accent marks explained (a full-text search for stress/accent the whole scanned for Accent/Betonung/betont: no hits). The only phonological remark is that Bunäj n corresponds to Carolinian m (p. 109, 'Yun' = 'Yum' house).
sources.venue: 'Notizen über einen Ausflug nach den westlichen Karolinen'

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page for mapi1250 (Mapia) and English Wikipedia 'Mapia language'.
sources.note: Nothing; Glottolog lists no descriptive reference (refs: Jackson 1983 classification comment, Campbell et al. 2022 AES, Lewis et al. 2015 'Dormant'); Wikipedia gives classification and extinction status only.

sources.citation: Bender, Byron W. 1975. Mapian: An extinct Micronesian language? Paper presented at the Second Annual Oceanic Linguistics Festival, Linguistic Society of Hawaii, Honolulu.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only dedicated linguistic study of Old Mapian; re-examines Kubary's data and might comment on his accent marks. Unpublished conference paper; possibly among Bender's papers at UH Manoa.

sources.citation: Bender, Byron W. 1971. Micronesian languages. In T. A. Sebeok (ed.), Current Trends in Linguistics 8: Linguistics in Oceania, 426-465. The Hague: Mouton.

sources.citation: Quackenbush, Edward Miller. 1968. From Sonsorol to Truk: a dialect chain. PhD dissertation, University of Michigan.

sources.note: Discusses Kubary's Mapia data (via Topping) and treats Trukic phonology, including stress, across the chain; may state or imply the pattern assumed for Mapian.

sources.access_detail: online with restricted access (login, paywall or limited view)
sources.note: Not verifiable from what was seen: a 70-page comparative study of Kubary's Mapia wordlist against other Chuukic languages; record and citations show no tone or prosody content, and none is expected for a wordlist-only extinct Chuukic language. Listed as the only modern linguistic analysis of Mapia not previously listed here (likely sound correspondences/lexicon), NOT as a countable tone work.
